translation: Arjuna said: O Janardana! If You consider wisdom superior to action, then why do You urge me to engage in this terrible, violent deed, O Keshava?
You puzzle my intellect with seemingly conflicting words. Tell me decisively that one single path by which I may attain the highest good.

The Blessed Lord said: O sinless one! In this world, a twofold path of spiritual practice was declared by Me in ancient times—the path of knowledge (Jnana-yoga) for the analytical thinkers (Sankhyas), and the path of selfless action (Karma-yoga) for the active practitioners (Yogis). Both paths are interdependent.
A person does not attain freedom from action (Naishkarmyam) merely by abstaining from the start of actions, nor does one reach perfection simply by formal renunciation (Sannyasana).
simple_explanation: Naishkarmya does not mean sitting idle like a fatalist. Performing good actions while dropping attachments is true freedom from action; absolute inaction is impossible.

translation: No one can remain even for a single moment without performing some action. Everyone is driven to act helplessly by the qualities born of nature (Gunas), such as hunger, thirst, or involuntary breathing.

He who restrains his physical organs of action (Karmendriyani) but continues to dwell on objects of the senses in his mind is a deluded soul, a practitioner of false conduct (Mithyacharah). He is deceiving himself.
But he who controls his senses through the mind, O Arjuna, and directs his physical organs to engage in the Yoga of selfless action without attachment, is highly distinguished.
Perform your prescribed duty (niyatam karma), for action is superior to inaction. Even the bare maintenance of your physical body (sharira-yatra) would be impossible through total inaction.
This world is bound by actions other than those performed for the sake of sacrifice (Yajna). Therefore, O son of Kunti, perform your action efficiently for that purpose, free from all attachment.
simple_explanation: What is Yajna? People mistake material fire-rituals for the complete definition. Material sacrifice is merely a symbolic drama, like a military parade before a battle. Its grammar reveals three roots: worship of wisdom-bearers, social organization, and charity. True Yajna is the harmonious organization of society. Living to serve society and eating what remains is eating Yajna-shesha. Living only to fill one's belly is cooking sin. Arjuna is a link in the sacrificial chain of the warrior class; he must fight to uphold justice without asking for personal prizes.

translation: In the beginning, having created mankind together with the principle of sacrifice (Yajna), Prajapati (the Creator) said: "By this sacrifice shall you multiply; let this be the wish-yielding cow of your desires (Kamadhuk)."
Foster the cosmic powers (Devas) with this sacrifice, and let those powers foster you. Fostering each other mutually, you shall attain the supreme good.
simple_explanation: Devas are of two kinds: living (parents, mentors, rulers) and insentient cosmic forces (earth, sun, rain). Insentient entities are worshiped by preserving them; for instance, the earth is nourished with organic fertilizer rather than just empty rituals.

translation: Nourished by sacrifice, the cosmic powers will bestow upon you your desired enjoyments. He who enjoys their gifts without offering anything in return to them is verily a thief (stena).
The righteous who consume the remnants of sacrifice (Yajna-shishta) are freed from all sins. But those sinful ones who cook food solely for their own selfish consumption eat only sin.
Living beings subsist on food, food is produced by rain, rain results from cosmic balance (Yajna), and sacrifice is born of right action (Karma).

Know that action originates from the Veda (the law of right order), and the Veda arises from the Imperishable Divine. Therefore, the all-pervading Cosmic Law (Sarvagatam Brahma) is eternally established in the spirit of sacrifice.
simple_explanation: Brahma here refers to the active law operating in the universe. Every section of society produces an asset, which is its "food." The coordinated labor of the workers is the "rain." When individuals cooperate, the "sacrifice" succeeds, supported by a structured chain of laws.

translation: He who does not follow the movement of the wheel of cosmic order thus set in motion in this life, lives a sinful life, indulging only his senses, O Partha. He lives in vain.
But for the human being who takes delight in the Self alone, who is completely satisfied with the Self, and content in the Self, there remains no personal obligation or binding duty to be performed.

He has no personal interest to gain by actions performed, nor does he lose anything by actions omitted. He does not depend on any created being for any personal objective. If others help him in public service, he welcomes them; if they do not, his enthusiasm does not break.
Therefore, remaining unattached, constantly perform that action which ought to be done (karyam karma); for by performing action without attachment, a person attains the Supreme.
simple_explanation: The key word here is Karyam (what is fit to be done). As stated later in 16.24, scripture and systemic laws are the authority in determining what is fit to be done (karya) and what is unfit (akarya). Once determined, execute it with detachment.

translation: King Janaka and others attained perfection through selfless action alone. Even with a view to the maintenance of world order and guidance of the people (Loka-sangraha), you should perform your duty.
Whatever a standard, leading person does, ordinary people mimic. Whatever standard of metrics he sets, the world follows that example.
There is no obligation for Me to perform any duty in all the three worlds, O Partha, nor is there anything unobtained for Me to obtain; yet I continue to engage in action.
For if I did not remain untiringly engaged in action, O Partha, all human beings would follow My path in every way and sink into inertia.
If I should cease to perform action, these worlds would fall into ruin. I would be the cause of social confusion (Sankara) and would destroy these creatures.
Just as the unwise perform actions with deep attachment to the results, O Bharata, the wise should act without attachment, desiring only the welfare and unity of the world.

The wise person should not unsettle the minds of ignorant people who are attached to ritualistic actions. Instead, acting with discipline and devotion, he should inspire them to enjoy and engage in all duties (joshayet).
All actions are performed in every way by the operational modes of material nature (Gunas). But he whose mind is utterly deluded by egotism thinks, "I am the independent author of this action."

But he who knows the ultimate truth regarding the separate jurisdictions of nature's modes and actions, O mighty-armed one, realizes that "it is merely the modes of nature interacting with their corresponding objects," and does not become attached to them.

Those deluded by the modes of material nature become attached to the operations of those modes. A person of complete knowledge should not disturb these dull-witted individuals of incomplete knowledge. Correct their attachment, not their habit of doing good work.
Surrendering all actions unto Me with a mind anchored in spirituality, free from expectation, free from selfishness, and cured of mental fever—fight!
Those human beings who constantly practice this teaching of Mine with full faith and free from cavil are also liberated from the binding effects of actions.
But those who out of envy mock and do not follow My teaching—know them to be completely devoid of wisdom, blind to reality, and ruined.

Even a well-informed person behaves in conformity with his own natural disposition and deeply ingrained habits. All living creatures follow their nature; what can mere temporary force or suppression achieve? Your Kshatriya nature will eventually wake up and force you to fight under worse terms if you run now.

Attraction and aversion are naturally embedded within the interaction of each sense organ with its corresponding object. One should never fall under their control, for they are the highway robbers (Paripanthinau) on one's spiritual path. Conquering family attachment is as crucial as conquering physical lust.

One's own dedicated duty (Svadharma), though imperfectly executed, is far better than the well-performed duty of another (Paradharma). Even death encountered while fulfilling one's own duty brings long-term credit; while the adoption of another's track is full of danger and fear.
Arjuna said: O Varshneya (Krishna)! Driven by what does a person commit sin, even against his own will, as if constrained by some external, overwhelming force?

The Blessed Lord said: It is desire (Kama), it is anger (Krodha), originating from the active mode of passion (Rajo-guna). It is insatiable like a blazing fire (mahashanah) and deeply sinful (maha-papma). Know this to be the principal enemy here in this world.
Just as fire is obscured by smoke, a mirror by dust, and an embryo by the amnion membrane, similarly, objective evaluation is obscured by this desire.
O son of Kunti! Wisdom is completely covered by this eternal enemy of the wise, which takes the form of desire and behaves like an insatiable fire.
The senses, the mind, and the intellect are declared to be its operational bases (adhishthanam). Covering wisdom through these three, it utterly bewilders the embodied soul.
Therefore, O foremost of the Bharata dynasty, master your senses first, and completely destroy this sinful agent, which demolishes both empirical knowledge (Jnana) and realized wisdom (Vijnana).

The sages say that the senses are superior to insentient matter; the mind is superior to the senses; the analytical intellect is superior to the mind; but that which is even superior to the intellect is the Soul (Atman).
Thus, knowing the Soul to be superior to the analytical intellect, steadying the lower self by the higher Self, O mighty-armed one, destroy this elusive enemy that takes the form of desire.
